topic: Day 2 · Acid–Base I — The Systematic Approach & Metabolic Acidosis
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: Acute physician and nephrologist who teaches the 'read any ABG in ninety seconds' course and believes the anion gap is the most under-used number on the shop floor.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 24-year-old woman is wheeled into resus drowsy and hyperventilating — deep, sighing Kussmaul breaths. The blood-gas machine spits out: pH 7.08, pCO₂ 2.1 kPa (16 mmHg), HCO₃⁻ 5 mmol/L, Na⁺ 138, Cl⁻ 100, glucose 34 mmol/L, ketones ++++. The registrar glances at the pH and says "she's acidotic, give bicarb." Stop. Before a single drop of anything, we are going to read this gas — properly, in the same order, every single time — because the numbers already tell you the diagnosis, the hidden second disorder, and whether she is compensating or crashing. This is the session where you learn to read any ABG in ninety seconds.

1 · 🧭 The five-step method — never freelance an ABG

The commonest way to misread a gas is to react to the first abnormal number you see. Discipline beats cleverness. Every gas, every time, in this order:

  1. Look at the pH — acidaemia (<7.35) or alkalaemia (>7.45)? This names the dominant process, even in a mixed picture.
  2. Identify the primary disorder — is the driver a change in HCO₃⁻ (metabolic) or in pCO₂ (respiratory)? The one that moves the pH in the observed direction is primary.
  3. Is compensation appropriate? Calculate the expected compensation. Too little or too much unmasks a second disorder.
  4. Calculate the anion gap (and correct it for albumin). A raised gap is a hard fact that survives every other manipulation.
  5. Delta-delta — in a high-gap acidosis, does the fall in bicarbonate match the rise in the gap? Mismatch = a third, coexisting disorder.
Don't treat the pH. Read the gas in the same five steps every time, and the diagnosis falls out of the numbers.
💡 Units — pick one and commit

pCO₂ in kPa × 7.5 = mmHg. A normal pCO₂ of 5.3 kPa is 40 mmHg. Winter's formula (below) is written for mmHg, so if your lab reports kPa, convert first or you will chase phantom respiratory disorders. Throughout this talk both units are given.

2 · ⚖️ Step 1–2: pH and the primary disorder

The Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship in one clinical sentence: pH tracks the ratio of bicarbonate (a metabolic, kidney-controlled base) to pCO₂ (a respiratory, lung-controlled acid). Four primary disorders fall straight out of it:

Primary disorderpHPrimary changeCompensation
Metabolic acidosis↓↓ HCO₃⁻↓ pCO₂ (hyperventilate)
Metabolic alkalosis↑↑ HCO₃⁻↑ pCO₂ (hypoventilate)
Respiratory acidosis↓↑ pCO₂↑ HCO₃⁻ (renal, slow)
Respiratory alkalosis↑↓ pCO₂↓ HCO₃⁻ (renal, slow)

The trick to naming the primary: the primary disorder and the pH move the same way. If the pH is low (acidaemia) and the HCO₃⁻ is low, the metabolic side is the driver. If the pH is low and the pCO₂ is high, the lung is the driver. Compensation never fully corrects the pH and never overshoots into the opposite abnormality — if it appears to, you have two primary disorders.

🎯 Compensation is not correction

The body defends pH but never returns it to 7.40 by compensation alone. A "normal" pH in a patient with a wildly abnormal HCO₃⁻ and pCO₂ is not a well patient — it is a mixed disorder with two processes cancelling out. Always finish the five steps even when the pH looks reassuring.

3 · 🌬️ Step 3: expected compensation — Winter's formula

For a metabolic acidosis, the lungs should blow off CO₂. How much is "right"? Winter's formula:

Expected pCO₂ (mmHg) = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (± 2).    Quick check: expected pCO₂ ≈ the last two digits of the pH.
  • Measured pCO₂ = expected → appropriate respiratory compensation; single metabolic acidosis.
  • Measured pCO₂ > expected → the patient is not blowing off enough CO₂ → a concurrent respiratory acidosis (tiring, opioids, CNS depression).
  • Measured pCO₂ < expected → blowing off too much → a concurrent respiratory alkalosis (sepsis, salicylate, pain, pregnancy).

Apply it to our opening case: HCO₃⁻ 5 → expected pCO₂ = 1.5 × 5 + 8 = 15.5 mmHg (~2.1 kPa). Measured is 16 mmHg — bang on. So this is a pure metabolic acidosis with fully appropriate respiratory compensation. Her lungs are working perfectly; do not intubate her for the low CO₂ — that CO₂ is keeping her alive.

⚠️ The intubation trap in severe metabolic acidosis

A DKA or salicylate patient may have a pCO₂ of 12–16 mmHg because they are hyperventilating heroically to defend pH. Sedate and paralyse them for intubation and their minute ventilation collapses; the ventilator rarely matches a spontaneous minute volume of 30+ L/min, pCO₂ rises, pH crashes, and cardiac arrest follows on induction. If you must tube, match their minute ventilation, keep them light, and consider awake technique. The respiratory drive is compensation, not a problem to fix.

4 · 🧮 Step 4: the anion gap — the unmeasured truth

Plasma is electroneutral. The anion gap exposes unmeasured anions:

AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻).   Normal ≈ 8–12 mmol/L (lab-dependent; if K⁺ is included, add ~4).

A metabolic acidosis raises the gap when the acid added brings its own unmeasured anion (lactate, ketoacids, glycolate). It leaves the gap normal when the lost bicarbonate is simply replaced by chloride (diarrhoea, RTA) — a "hyperchloraemic" acidosis. This single fork organises the entire differential.

Correct the gap for albumin — the step everyone forgets

Albumin is the dominant unmeasured anion. A hypoalbuminaemic ICU patient has a low baseline gap, so a "normal" gap of 12 may actually be dangerously high. Correct it:

Corrected AG = measured AG + 2.5 × (40 − albumin in g/L)/10  (i.e. +2.5 for every 10 g/L of albumin below 40).
💡 The albumin correction saves lives in the ICU

An albumin of 20 g/L drops the expected gap by ~5. A septic patient with a measured gap of 11 and albumin 20 has a corrected gap of ~16 — a genuine high-gap acidosis (probably lactate) that the raw number hides completely. Always correct before you call a gap "normal."

5 · 🔥 High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) — GOLD MARK

MUDPILES is the old mnemonic; the cleaner modern one is GOLD MARK (Mehta). Every entry adds an organic or fixed acid with an unmeasured anion:

LetterCauseUnmeasured anion / mechanism
GGlycols (ethylene glycol, propylene glycol)Glycolate, oxalate; propylene glycol (drug diluent) → lactate
OOxoproline (pyroglutamic acid)Chronic paracetamol + malnutrition/sepsis in women
LL-lactateType A (hypoperfusion/hypoxia) & Type B (metformin, liver failure, malignancy)
DD-lactateShort-bowel/bacterial overgrowth — normal L-lactate assay misses it
MMethanolFormic acid → retinal toxicity (blindness)
AAspirin (salicylate)Uncouples oxidative phosphorylation; also drives respiratory alkalosis
RRenal failure (uraemia)Retained sulphate, phosphate, urate
KKetoacidosisβ-hydroxybutyrate — diabetic, alcoholic, starvation

The big three by mechanism

  • Lactate — the anaerobic emergency. Type A = oxygen delivery failure (shock, hypoxaemia, mesenteric ischaemia). Type B = normal delivery but deranged metabolism (metformin accumulation in AKI, thiamine deficiency, lymphoma, mitochondrial toxins). Lactate >4 mmol/L in sepsis is a resuscitation trigger; a clearing lactate is the single best sign your resuscitation is working.
  • Ketones — insulin lack (DKA) or glycogen depletion (alcoholic/starvation ketoacidosis) shifts fatty-acid metabolism to β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate. Note: the urine nitroprusside dipstick detects acetoacetate, not β-hydroxybutyrate — early DKA with a redox state favouring β-OHB can show falsely low ketones. Measure blood β-hydroxybutyrate.
  • Toxic alcohols — methanol and ethylene glycol: parent alcohol raises the osmolar gap early; hepatic metabolism to formic/glycolic acid then raises the anion gap late (covered in depth in session 16).
🎯 Osmolar gap — the HAGMA you cannot see on the anion gap yet

Calculated osmolality = 2×Na⁺ + glucose + urea (all mmol/L). Measured − calculated > 10 mOsm/kg = an osmolar gap, signalling an unmeasured small molecule: methanol, ethylene glycol, or a large ethanol load. Early toxic-alcohol poisoning has a high osmolar gap and a normal anion gap; hours later, as it is metabolised, the osmolar gap closes and the anion gap opens. Catch it early — see session 16.

6 · 🧂 Normal-anion-gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis — NAGMA

Here bicarbonate is lost and chloride rises to fill the electrical gap, so the AG stays normal. The mnemonic USED CARP (Ureteric diversion, Small-bowel fistula, Extra chloride/saline, Diarrhoea, Carbonic-anhydrase inhibitors, Adrenal insufficiency, Renal tubular acidosis, Pancreatic fistula) covers it, but clinically it collapses to one question: is the bicarbonate leaking from the gut or the kidney?

The urine anion gap — GI vs renal in one calculation

Urine AG = UNa + UK − UCl.   Think of it as a proxy for urinary ammonium (NH₄⁺), the kidney's acid-excreting workhorse.
  • NEGATIVE urine AG (e.g. −20 to −50) = lots of NH₄Cl in the urine = the kidney is appropriately excreting acid = the problem is outside the kidney → diarrhoea (or other GI bicarbonate loss). "NEGative = GUT / NEGUTIVE."
  • POSITIVE urine AG = the kidney is failing to make ammonium = the acidification defect is renal → renal tubular acidosis.
💡 NEGUTIVE

A NEGative urine anion gap points to the GUT. Remember "NEG-UT-IVE." A positive value points to the kidney (RTA). It works because the calculation estimates unmeasured NH₄⁺: a healthy kidney facing acidosis floods the urine with ammonium chloride, making the measured Cl⁻ exceed Na⁺+K⁺.

Renal tubular acidosis — the three types you must separate

FeatureType 1 (distal)Type 2 (proximal)Type 4 (hyperkalaemic)
DefectDistal H⁺ secretion failsProximal HCO₃⁻ reabsorption failsAldosterone deficiency/resistance
Serum K⁺LowLowHigh
Urine pH>5.5 (can't acidify)Variable; <5.5 once HCO₃⁻ depleted<5.5
Serum HCO₃⁻Can be very low (<10)Usually 12–20Mild (16–22)
Classic causeSjögren, RA, amphotericinFanconi, myeloma, acetazolamideDiabetes, ACE-i/ARB, NSAIDs, spironolactone
ComplicationNephrocalcinosis, stonesRickets/osteomalaciaManage the hyperkalaemia
Type 1 can't acidify the distal urine (pH high, K low); Type 2 wastes bicarbonate proximally (K low); Type 4 is the low-aldosterone one with HIGH potassium.

7 · 🔺 Step 5: delta-delta — the hidden second disorder

In a pure HAGMA, every mmol of acid added should consume one mmol of bicarbonate: the rise in the anion gap should equal the fall in the bicarbonate. The delta ratio tests this:

Δ ratio = (measured AG − 12) ÷ (24 − measured HCO₃⁻).
Δ ratioInterpretation
< 0.4Bicarbonate fell far more than the gap rose → coexisting normal-gap acidosis
0.4 – 1Mixed high-gap AND normal-gap acidosis
1 – 2Pure high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
> 2Gap rose more than bicarbonate fell → coexisting metabolic alkalosis or pre-existing high HCO₃⁻ (chronic respiratory acidosis)
🎯 Why this matters at the bedside

A vomiting DKA patient can have a delta ratio >2: the ketoacidosis raises the gap, but the vomiting-induced metabolic alkalosis props the bicarbonate up so the pH and HCO₃⁻ look deceptively "not that bad." The delta-delta is what tells you there is a second process you would otherwise miss — and warns you the bicarbonate will crash once the vomiting is treated and the alkalosis lifts.

8 · 🧑‍⚕️ Two worked examples — the method in action

Example A — the opening case

pH 7.08, pCO₂ 16 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 5, Na 138, Cl 100.

  1. pH 7.08 → acidaemia.
  2. HCO₃⁻ 5 (low) with low pH → metabolic acidosis is primary.
  3. Winter's: expected pCO₂ = 1.5×5 + 8 = 15.5. Measured 16 → appropriate compensation, no respiratory disorder.
  4. AG = 138 − (100 + 5) = 33 → high-anion-gap. With ketones ++++ and glucose 34 → DKA.
  5. Δ ratio = (33−12)/(24−5) = 21/19 = 1.1 → pure HAGMA. No hidden second disorder.

Diagnosis: pure high-gap metabolic acidosis due to DKA, fully compensated. Treatment is fluids, insulin, and potassium — not bicarbonate, and definitely not intubation.

Example B — the "not that sick" trap

An alcoholic man: pH 7.30, pCO₂ 40 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 19, Na 140, Cl 92, albumin 28 g/L.

  1. pH 7.30 → mild acidaemia.
  2. HCO₃⁻ 19 (low) → metabolic acidosis primary.
  3. Winter's: expected pCO₂ = 1.5×19 + 8 = 36.5. Measured 40 → slightly high → a touch of respiratory acidosis too.
  4. AG = 140 − (92 + 19) = 29. Corrected for albumin: +2.5×(40−28)/10 = +3 → corrected AG ~32 — a big high-gap acidosis (alcoholic ketoacidosis + lactate) despite the almost-normal bicarbonate.
  5. Δ ratio = (32−12)/(24−19) = 20/5 = 4 → >2 = coexisting metabolic alkalosis (he has been vomiting).

Diagnosis: a triple disorder — high-gap metabolic acidosis + metabolic alkalosis + mild respiratory acidosis — in a man whose pH of 7.30 and bicarbonate of 19 look almost benign. The five-step method is the only thing that finds all three.

☠️ M&M — the bicarbonate that stopped the heart

A 19-year-old in DKA arrived with pH 6.95 and a pCO₂ of 14 mmHg. A well-meaning night SHO, alarmed by the pH, pushed 200 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate. Within twenty minutes the patient became more obtunded and arrested. What happened: the bolus of CO₂-generating bicarbonate crossed the blood–brain barrier faster than the bicarbonate did, causing a paradoxical CNS acidosis; it drove potassium intracellularly precipitating a fatal arrhythmia in an already total-body-K-depleted patient; and it shifted the oxygen-dissociation curve worsening tissue oxygen delivery. Lessons: the low pCO₂ was appropriate compensation, not a target; DKA is treated with fluid, insulin and potassium, not bicarbonate; bicarbonate in high-gap ketoacidosis is reserved (controversially) for pH <6.9 or life-threatening hyperkalaemia, and even then given as a slow diluted infusion with obsessive potassium monitoring. He treated the number on the screen instead of reading the gas.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Five steps, same order, every gas: pH → primary disorder → expected compensation → anion gap (albumin-corrected) → delta-delta.
  2. Winter's formula (expected pCO₂ = 1.5×HCO₃⁻ + 8) tells you if the lungs are compensating right — deviation means a second, respiratory disorder.
  3. Correct the anion gap for albumin (+2.5 per 10 g/L below 40) or you will miss a real high-gap acidosis in every hypoalbuminaemic patient.
  4. HAGMA = GOLD MARK — think lactate, ketones, toxic alcohols, uraemia and salicylate first; each brings its own unmeasured anion.
  5. NAGMA = gut vs kidney, split by the urine anion gap: NEGative → GUT (diarrhoea); positive → RTA. Type 1 can't acidify (low K), Type 2 wastes bicarb (low K), Type 4 is the high-K one.
  6. Delta-delta unmasks the hidden disorder: <1 adds a normal-gap acidosis, >2 adds a metabolic alkalosis.
  7. Never treat the pH. The compensatory low pCO₂ in a severe metabolic acidosis is keeping the patient alive — do not sedate it away.

moderatorQs.q: A patient has a metabolic acidosis with HCO₃⁻ of 10. Their pCO₂ is 40 mmHg. Is that reassuring?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — it is alarming. Winter's formula gives an expected pCO₂ of 1.5×10 + 8 = 23 mmHg (≈3.1 kPa) for appropriate respiratory compensation. A measured pCO₂ of 40 means the patient is failing to blow off CO₂ — a superimposed respiratory acidosis. In a metabolic acidosis a 'normal' pCO₂ is a red flag for a tiring, obtunded or opioid-affected patient who is about to decompensate. I would look hard for the cause of ventilatory failure, support ventilation, and escalate — that number is a pre-arrest warning, not reassurance.

moderatorQs.q: How does the urine anion gap distinguish diarrhoea from renal tubular acidosis in a normal-gap acidosis?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The urine anion gap (UNa + UK − UCl) is a bedside proxy for urinary ammonium, the kidney's main way of excreting acid. In diarrhoea the kidney is healthy and responds to acidosis by pouring out NH₄Cl, so chloride exceeds sodium plus potassium and the urine AG is strongly negative (remember 'NEG-UT-IVE' — negative points to the gut). In renal tubular acidosis the kidney cannot generate ammonium, so the urine AG is positive. So a negative value says the acidosis is GI in origin; a positive value says the defect is renal and sends you to sub-type the RTA (urine pH, serum potassium).

moderatorQs.q: You calculate a delta ratio of 4 in a patient with a high-gap acidosis. What does that tell you?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A delta ratio (ΔAG ÷ ΔHCO₃⁻) greater than 2 means the anion gap has risen much more than the bicarbonate has fallen — the bicarbonate is being propped up by a coexisting process. That is either a concurrent metabolic alkalosis (classically the vomiting DKA patient) or a pre-existing high bicarbonate from chronic respiratory acidosis (COPD). Clinically it warns you the true severity of the acid load is masked, and that the bicarbonate may fall sharply once the alkalosis is corrected — so you keep replacing potassium and watching the gas rather than being reassured by a near-normal HCO₃⁻.

audienceQs.q: Why shouldn't I just give bicarbonate to a patient with a pH of 7.0 in DKA?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because in high-gap ketoacidosis bicarbonate does more harm than good. The low pH is driven by ketoacids that clear rapidly with insulin and fluid — fix the metabolism and the pH self-corrects. Pushed bicarbonate generates CO₂ that crosses into the CNS causing a paradoxical cerebral acidosis, drives potassium intracellularly in a patient who is already total-body potassium depleted (risking a fatal arrhythmia), and can worsen tissue oxygen delivery. Guidelines reserve it — controversially — for pH <6.9 or life-threatening hyperkalaemia, given slowly, diluted, with obsessive potassium monitoring. For everyone else: fluids, insulin, potassium, and patience.

audienceQs.q: My septic patient has a 'normal' anion gap of 11 but looks acidotic. What am I missing?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Almost certainly the albumin correction. Albumin is the largest unmeasured anion, so a hypoalbuminaemic ICU patient has a low baseline gap and a raised gap gets hidden. Correct it: add 2.5 for every 10 g/L of albumin below 40. If this patient's albumin is 20, the correction is +5, giving a corrected gap of ~16 — a genuine high-anion-gap acidosis, in a septic patient almost certainly lactate. Check a lactate, re-examine perfusion and source control, and don't let the raw number falsely reassure you.

audienceQs.q: Which drugs should I flag as causes of a metabolic acidosis on the drug chart?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Plenty. For a high-gap acidosis: metformin (type B lactic acidosis, especially when it accumulates in AKI), and toxic ingestions — salicylate and the toxic alcohols. Chronic paracetamol in a malnourished patient causes pyroglutamic (5-oxoproline) acidosis. For a normal-gap acidosis: acetazolamide and topiramate (carbonic-anhydrase inhibition), and the type-4 RTA drugs — ACE inhibitors/ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim and NSAIDs — which cause a hyperkalaemic acidosis by reducing aldosterone effect. I'd flag metformin for suspension in any acute kidney injury and review the potassium-raising combinations.
